answers.displayAnswer: Forced electrical oscillations occur when a circuit is continuously driven by an externally applied, periodically varying electromotive force or voltage. In the steady forced response, the oscillation frequency equals the driving frequency. In a passive circuit with losses, the external source supplies enough energy each cycle to replace the energy lost during that cycle. Charging a capacitor only once produces a free response, not sustained forced oscillations.

For a pure resistor with fixed resistance $R$, Ohm's law holds at every instant: $u(t)=Ri(t)$, or $i(t)=u(t)/R$. Sinusoidal current and voltage have the same frequency and phase: they cross zero together and reach their respective positive and negative peaks at the same times. Their amplitudes and RMS values also satisfy $U_{\mathrm{m}}=RI_{\mathrm{m}}$ and $U=RI$.

For a sinusoidal voltage averaged over a complete cycle, $U=U_{\mathrm{m}}/\sqrt{2}$, so its amplitude is $U_{\mathrm{m}}=\sqrt{2}U$. In the stated order, the amplitudes are $220\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{V}\approx311\,\mathrm{V}$ and $127\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{V}\approx180\,\mathrm{V}$. The approximations are to the nearest whole volt. Amplitude is neither RMS voltage nor peak-to-peak voltage. This is a calculation on paper, not a circuit measurement.

Over a specified time interval, RMS current is the nonnegative square root of the time average of the squared instantaneous current: $I=\sqrt{\overline{i^2}}$. RMS voltage is defined in the same way: $U=\sqrt{\overline{u^2}}$. First square the instantaneous values, then average over time, then take the nonnegative square root. For periodic AC, the average is usually taken over a complete cycle. RMS is neither the signed mean nor the peak value. For the sinusoidal waves in this lesson, $I=I_{\mathrm{m}}/\sqrt{2}$ and $U=U_{\mathrm{m}}/\sqrt{2}$.
